items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' The courtesy check — 'Is it the convenient time to talk?' — is good practice on an outbound call and is not the same as a warm-up.

The moving-stressor question was never asked. This is the only real gap in an otherwise excellent probe: the customer was asked about items, access, walk distance, gates and boxes, and never once asked what she was worried about.

The hourly rate was never stated. Not per mover, not per team, not at all. The customer was told 'The estimated cost is $929' for a four-hour move and left to reverse-engineer a rate she was never given. She cannot compare this quote to a competitor's, cannot check the math, and cannot tell what a fifth hour would cost her.

What's-included was never stated. No gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no wrap, pads, bands, or tools. On a six-and-a-half-minute call that collected an unusually detailed inventory, the customer never heard a single thing about what her money buys.

Disassembly and reassembly never mentioned. The inventory includes a mattress, a dresser, two desks and a table with chairs — most of that needs tools — and the customer never learned it is included at no cost.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The load includes two couches, a 50-inch TV and a dresser coming down three flights of exterior stairs. No $2,000, no repair-replace-reimburse, no 60c/lb baseline, no mention of coverage in any form.
The no-hidden-fees pitch never delivered — not the claim and not the list.

Meet Your Mover was described mechanically but never named or completed: 'normally two to three days prior to remove, we will already send you the name of the mirrors [movers], the day before we already doing courtesy call or text just to remind you and on the day itself we will give you estimated time of arrival.' The timing is right and the names are right; the feature is never named and the mover's photo — the part that actually does the reassurance work — is never mentioned. The flag reads false because the differentiator was never explicitly identified as such.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, and this is the single most costly miss in this week's entire sample because the customer asked for it directly. Her words: 'their estimated time of arrival, I saw that I booked 8:30 and it said they would let us know if it's like within, if they're like running late or if there's traffic about like thirty minutes late or something like that, is that still accurate?' That is a customer volunteering a concern about lateness and inviting the differentiator built to answer it. The reply was 'That is correct. So normally, that would be from 8:30 AM to 9:00 AM the, that's the earliest that we can do.' The answer was procedural, the reassurance never came, and the opening closed.

The clock section is almost entirely missing. The 2.5-hour minimum was never stated in hours, the fifteen-minute proration was never mentioned, and when billable time starts was never explained. The only trace is a garbled reference — 'in case you end up only the minimum it's $2,620' — which gives a number for a minimum the customer was never told the length of.
No sense-check anywhere on the call.

No typical time range was given for the home size. The four-hour figure was asserted with no benchmark for a one-bedroom apartment, so the customer cannot judge whether the three flights of stairs are what pushed it there.

The three-flight walk-up was captured perfectly in the probe and then never explained as the reason for the estimate. Roselyn established 'This is located on the third floor. No elevator [only] stairs' and pinned the walk at 'twenty to fifty feet and that's accounting for the stairs to go up' — and then the estimate arrived as a bare four hours with no connection drawn. The customer never learned that her stairs are the biggest single driver of her bill, which is exactly the information that would make her prep harder.
Assembly and disassembly never explained as an estimate variable.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used, despite the customer having already anchored herself to a range she found in the booking form.

The 'take a carload' tip was never given, and no consolidation examples beyond one. The prep speech landed its core logic but stopped at 'put the small items into your boxes yourself' — no kids' items, no garden tools, no loose items in drawers, no photos off the walls, and no 'anything small can go in your car.' On a move with three flights of exterior stairs and no elevator, the carload tip is worth more than on any other call this week.
No 'does that make sense?' close on the prep speech — it was delivered inside a run-on sentence and never landed as a distinct piece of advice.
No deposit required never mentioned.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email, and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. What the customer got was 'I'll send you a confirmation email and if ever there will be changes with regards to the date and the time, just let us know' — a channel for changing the booking, not a request to verify the record. On a call that captured a gate buzz-in procedure, two unit-level walk distances, a corrected floor plan and a box count, the verification loop is what protects all of it.

No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The call went from a garbled pricing block straight to 'Alright then. Thank you so much and happy Sunday. Bye-bye.' The customer had just received a $929 figure with no rate, no inclusions and no differentiators attached to it, and was never given an opening to ask about any of that.
No hours and no direct number given at close.
Customer's name used twice — 'I'm looking to speak with Emma' and 'Hi, Emma' — both in the opening, neither during the substance of the call.
No rapport or lightness anywhere; the register is procedural start to finish.
top_strength: Roselyn runs the most disciplined probe in this week's sample, and she does it in six and a half minutes, which is the shortest call in the batch. She asked the access question in better language than anyone else used: 'do we have access concerns, like narrow pathways and hallways, steep driveways...' — and then worked the answer all the way through. The customer mentioned a gate, and rather than noting it and moving on, Roselyn chased the actual mechanism until she had something the crew could use on move day: 'let me just go ahead and put it here so there's like, there's a gate code,' which produced 'There's not a gate code, like essentially when the movers get there, they could either call me or text me and I can buzz them in from my phone or there's a call box next to the gate and they just search my name.' That is a real move-day failure prevented in the file. She measured the walk in two directions at the origin, which nobody else attempted: 'What's the walk distance from where we can park the truck to the bottom of the stairs and from the top of the stairs going to the front door' — splitting the ground-level approach from the stair climb — and then repeated the question at the destination. She asked the heavy-items and the fragile-items questions as two separate passes, both specific: 'do we have anything larger heavy, like safe piano large workout equipment, washers dryers TV' and then 'do we have anything valuable or fragile like antique collection, artwork collection, anything made of marble, granite or glass.' She asked about additional rooms and caught the office. She confirmed no packing help was needed. She benchmarked the box count against the home size rather than asking an open question ('a typical box count for your home size is fifteen to 25 boxes. Do you feel that you fall within that range?'). And she is the only rep in this week's sample to attempt the Save Your Ass speech at all. It is short and it is buried in a run-on, but the core logic is there and it is correct: 'in case if you still have extra time just to prepare but [put] the small items into your boxes yourself that would really help to keep the time down and efficiency up. Obviously the less time you take, the less money you end up spending by the end of the day.' That is prep-equals-shorter-move-equals-lower-bill, said to a customer with three flights of stairs and no elevator, which is where it pays the most. She also opened the call properly — stated why she was calling, what she would do, and asked permission to proceed — and she is one of only two reps this week to state both the mover count and the truck count explicitly.
coaching_note: The pattern on this call is unusually clean and worth showing Roselyn directly: she collected the best information in the batch and then delivered almost none of the value. Probe 8/9, pricing 5/20, clock 1/4. She knows this customer is on a third floor with no exterior elevator, has a twenty-to-fifty-foot stair walk, two couches, a 50-inch TV, fifteen to twenty boxes and a gate that requires a phone buzz-in — and the customer walked away knowing one number, $929, with no hourly rate, no inclusions, no coverage, no minimum, no proration, and no idea that her stairs are the reason the estimate is four hours instead of three. Highest-leverage fix: state the rate and connect the estimate to the variables you already collected. 'Two movers and one truck at [rate] per mover per hour. For a one-bedroom like yours we'd normally be looking at about three hours, but the third floor with no elevator and the stair walk is what takes this to four — that's about $929. If we come in under, you only pay for what we use.' That single paragraph gives her the rate, the typical range, the reason, and the downside protection, and it turns the stairs from a hidden cost into something she can act on. Second priority, and this one should sting a little: the customer asked for the On-Time Guarantee out loud. She raised the arrival window, said she had read something about being notified if the crew runs thirty minutes late, and asked 'is that still accurate?' The answer was a flat restatement of the window. The line was right there: 'That's right — and more than that, we have an on-time guarantee. If we miss that window we start discounting your move from the start, because we know how much a late crew throws off your day.' That is the differentiator handed over on a plate and dropped. Third, the Save Your Ass attempt deserves real credit — it is the only one in the sample — and it needs about fifteen more seconds to actually work. Right now it is a subordinate clause inside a sentence that also contains the estimate, the total, and the rescheduling policy. Pull it out, give it examples, add the carload tip, and close it: 'One thing that'll save you real money here — with three flights and no elevator, every trip up and down costs time. Anything small you can carry down yourself before Saturday helps: the loose stuff in drawers, anything off the walls, closet odds and ends. If you can take a carload or two over in your own car, even better. Does that make sense?' Fourth: the close is abrupt. She delivered a $929 number with no rate attached and hung up eleven seconds later with no questions check and no deposit reassurance. Add 'Any other questions before I let you go?' and 'There's no deposit — you don't pay anything until the move is done.' No estimate-accuracy flag on the number itself: four hours for a 1,000-square-foot one-bedroom coming down three unelevatored flights with fifteen to twenty boxes is defensible and is not padded. The accuracy failure here is a communication failure, not a math one — the customer cannot verify a quote whose inputs and rate she was never given, and a customer who does not understand what drives her hours cannot help bring them down. The agenda opener is a genuine hit and is worth naming as the model for outbound calls: 'we just wanted to ask you some information in order for us to give you a perfect quote. Is it the convenient time to talk?' states the purpose, states what will happen, and asks for confirmation. Adding the pricing preview and the ten-to-fifteen-minute timeframe would make it complete.
phone_presence_notes: Courteous and efficient with a polite open and close ('Is it the convenient time to talk?' / 'Thank you so much and happy Sunday'), but the register is transactional from start to finish: the name is used twice and both times in the first two lines, acknowledgments are almost entirely 'Okay' and 'Okay, no worries,' the customer's mild concern about a late crew drew a procedural answer with no empathy and no reassurance, and the call ends eleven seconds after a $929 figure with no invitation to react to it.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on transcript evidence that is too degraded to rely on alone. The entire closing block — which carries the estimate, the prep advice, the minimum and the rescheduling policy — renders as one run-on with multiple unrecoverable passages: 'estimated time is four hours. The estimated cost is $929 then again we're timely based so in case if you still have extra time just to prepare but in the small items into your boxes yourself... in case you end up only the minimum it's $2,620,' and earlier 'we will already send you the name of the mirrors.' Audio is needed to determine whether the customer actually received a coherent estimate and a usable prep tip, what the minimum figure really was, and whether the flat delivery is real or an artifact of a sparse transcript.
